title: Reporting online financial fraud (1930 and cybercrime.gov.in)
text: If money was taken from your account through an online scam, call the national cyber crime helpline 1930 immediately — reporting within the first few hours (the golden hour) lets banks freeze the fraudulent transaction chain. Also file a written complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal at cybercrime.gov.in with transaction IDs, screenshots and the fraudster's number or UPI ID. You do not need to visit a police station first, and you may additionally file a Zero FIR at any police station. Online cheating is punishable under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000.

title: Filing a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal
text: cybercrime.gov.in lets any citizen register a complaint under three broad categories: Report Women/Children Related Crime, Report Financial Fraud, and Report Other Cyber Crimes; the first two categories also allow anonymous reporting. Create an account or file anonymously, describe the incident, attach evidence such as screenshots and transaction references, and submit — the portal issues an acknowledgement number you can use to track your complaint status online. Complaints registered here are automatically routed to the concerned state cyber cell for investigation, so a police-station visit is not a precondition for filing.

title: "Digital arrest" scams — there is no such thing in Indian law
text: In this scam, callers impersonate police, CBI, RBI, customs or narcotics officers on a video call and claim you are under "digital arrest", pressuring you to stay on camera and transfer money to "clear" a fake case. The Government of India has clarified that no law provides for arrest over a phone or video call, and no investigating agency conducts interrogation or demands money this way. If this happens: do not pay, disconnect the call, inform family, call the national cyber helpline 1930, and file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in with the caller's number and any recording.

title: Responding to sextortion and blackmail threats
text: Sextortion is when someone threatens to share intimate images or videos of you unless you pay money or send more content; it is criminal extortion under Section 308 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and can also involve criminal intimidation under Section 351. Do not pay and do not delete the chats, screenshots or the profile — preserve them as evidence. Report immediately at cybercrime.gov.in (the Women/Children category allows anonymous filing) or call 1930. You may also approach the local police or cyber cell directly; blocking the contact after saving evidence is advisable.

title: Reporting a hacked social media or email account
text: If your Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp or email account has been taken over, first use the platform's own account-recovery/"my account was hacked" flow to attempt to regain access, and alert your contacts that the account is compromised so they do not fall for messages sent from it. Change passwords on any linked accounts and enable two-factor authentication once recovered. File a complaint under the "Report Other Cyber Crimes" category at cybercrime.gov.in with the account URL/handle and any ransom or impersonation messages; unauthorised access to a computer resource is punishable under the Information Technology Act, 2000.

title: Reporting morphed images and non-consensual intimate imagery
text: Circulating a woman's photo after morphing it into an obscene image, or capturing/sharing a private image without consent, is punishable as voyeurism under Section 77 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and as a violation of privacy under Section 66E of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Take screenshots of the content and the sharer's profile/URL before it is taken down, then file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in under the Women/Children Related Crime category (anonymous filing is available) or call 1930; the platform can separately be asked to remove the content under its own reporting tools.

title: Reporting online job and work-from-home fraud
text: Fraudulent job offers that demand an upfront "registration", "training" or "equipment" fee, or task-based work-from-home schemes that ask you to keep investing money to "unlock" earnings, are cheating offences under Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 when committed online. Stop all further payments immediately, save the job advertisement, chat history, and payment/transaction records, and report at cybercrime.gov.in under Financial Fraud or call 1930 if money was transferred. Verify any recruiter independently through the company's official website or HR contact before paying anything.

title: Recovering money sent to the wrong UPI ID or account
text: If you transferred money to the wrong UPI ID, phone number or account by mistake, contact your bank's customer care or the UPI app's support immediately and request a reversal — banks can raise a dispute with the beneficiary bank, though the receiver's consent is generally needed to actually return the funds if they do not cooperate. If the recipient refuses to return an accidental transfer, you can lodge a complaint with your bank's grievance redressal officer, escalate to the RBI Banking Ombudsman, or pursue the matter as a civil claim; if there are signs of deliberate fraud, report it at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930.

title: SIM-swap fraud — recognising and reporting it
text: In a SIM-swap fraud, criminals get a duplicate SIM issued for your number (often using your personal details or a fake ID) and then use OTPs sent to that SIM to access your bank or wallet accounts; a warning sign is your phone suddenly losing network/signal for no reason. If this happens, contact your telecom operator immediately to block the SIM and your bank to freeze the account, then call the cyber helpline 1930 and file a complaint at cybercrime.gov.in with your telecom and bank details; unauthorised access and cheating using a computer resource are punishable under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Section 318 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

title: Cyber cell versus the local police station — where to go
text: You are not required to find the "right" office before reporting a cyber offence: any police station must register information about a cognizable offence irrespective of where it occurred (Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, the Zero FIR rule), and cyber crimes are cognizable when they involve fraud, cheating or similar offences. In practice, the fastest route for financial cyber fraud is the national helpline 1930 and the cybercrime.gov.in portal, which routes your complaint directly to the dedicated cyber cell of the state concerned; you may still additionally register a Zero FIR at any local police station for the same incident.

title: Preserving evidence before filing a cyber complaint
text: Before you file a cyber crime complaint, preserve everything that shows what happened: full-screen screenshots of chats, profiles and payment screens (including date/time stamps), the sender's phone number/UPI ID/account number, bank SMS alerts, the exact transaction ID (UTR/RRN) for each disputed payment, and the URL of any fake website or app used. Do not delete the app, block the contact, or uninstall anything until you have saved this material, since cybercrime.gov.in and the investigating cyber cell will ask for these details, and electronic records are admissible as evidence when properly certified.

title: IT Act versus BNS charges for online cheating — how they combine
text: Online cheating is usually charged under both laws together, not one instead of the other: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 supplies the general cheating offence (Section 318, covering deception that dishonestly induces a person to part with property), while the Information Technology Act, 2000 supplies offences specific to the digital method used — Section 66C for identity theft (misuse of a password/electronic signature), Section 66D for cheating by personation using a computer resource, and Section 66E for privacy violations. A single online fraud FIR commonly cites sections from both statutes together.

title: Zero FIR — filing an FIR at any police station
text: A Zero FIR can be registered at ANY police station regardless of where the offence happened; the station records it with serial number zero and transfers it to the station with jurisdiction. Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 obliges the officer in charge to record information about a cognizable offence irrespective of the area where it was committed, and information may also be given electronically (e-FIR). Registration is free and you are entitled to a free copy of the FIR. If the police refuse, send your complaint in writing to the Superintendent of Police, and thereafter you may approach the Magistrate.

title: e-FIR — giving information about a cognizable offence electronically
text: Section 173(1)(ii) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 allows information about a cognizable offence to be given "by electronic communication" and not only in person; if given electronically, it must be signed by the informant within three days of the officer taking it on record. Many state police departments run an e-FIR/online-complaint portal for specific categories such as vehicle theft or lost property, after which you visit the station to sign the recorded statement. This does not replace the option of walking into any police station, including for a Zero FIR.

title: FIR registration and your copy are both free
text: No fee is charged for registering an FIR, and Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires the officer in charge to record information about a cognizable offence as given; the informant is entitled to receive a free copy of the FIR once it is registered. If an officer demands money to register a complaint or to hand over the FIR copy, that itself can be reported to the Superintendent of Police or the District Magistrate, and refusal to perform an official duty without reasonable cause can attract action against the officer.

title: What to do when police refuse to register an FIR
text: If an officer in charge refuses to record information about a cognizable offence, Section 173(4) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 lets the aggrieved person send the substance of the information in writing, by post, to the Superintendent of Police, who must either investigate personally or direct a subordinate officer to investigate. Separately, Section 175(3) allows an application (supported by an affidavit) to a Magistrate empowered under Section 210, who can, after inquiry, direct the police to register and investigate the case. Keep a copy of your written complaint and any acknowledgment as proof of the refusal.

title: Your rights at the time of arrest
text: Section 47 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires the arresting officer to communicate, at the time of arrest, the full particulars of the offence or other grounds for the arrest; if the offence is bailable, the person must also be told that they are entitled to be released on bail and may arrange sureties. Section 48 further requires the police to inform a relative, friend, or another person nominated by the arrested person about the arrest and the place of custody, and to make an entry of this in the police station's register.

title: Women cannot generally be arrested after sunset or before sunrise
text: Section 43(5) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides that, save in exceptional circumstances, no woman shall be arrested after sunset and before sunrise; where such exceptional circumstances exist, a woman police officer must, by written report, first obtain the prior permission of a first-class Magistrate having local jurisdiction. This is a safeguard, not an absolute bar — the Magistrate's permission can still authorise a night arrest in genuinely exceptional situations, but the default rule protects women from being taken into custody overnight.

title: The 24-hour rule — production before a Magistrate
text: Section 58 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires that a person arrested without a warrant not be detained for more than twenty-four hours (excluding travel time to court) without being produced before a Magistrate; Section 187 sets out what the police must do if the investigation cannot be finished within that period — the officer must forward the accused and the case diary entries to the nearest Magistrate, who can then authorise further custody. Any detention beyond twenty-four hours without a Magistrate's order is illegal.

title: A woman's arrest — who may touch her, and the presumption of submission
text: Section 43(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides that, unless circumstances indicate otherwise, a woman being arrested is presumed to submit to custody on an oral intimation of arrest, and — unless circumstances otherwise require or the police officer herself is a woman — a male officer shall not touch the woman to effect the arrest. In practice this means arrests of women should ordinarily be carried out or physically effected by women police personnel, with physical restraint on a non-consenting woman by a male officer being the exception rather than the rule.

title: Bail in bailable offences is a matter of right
text: Section 478 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 provides that a person accused of a bailable offence who is arrested or appears before a court and is prepared to give bail SHALL be released on bail — this is not left to the discretion of the police officer or the court. If the person is indigent and cannot furnish a surety, the officer or court may release them on executing a bond without sureties. For non-bailable offences, Section 480 governs when bail may (not must) be granted, and is subject to conditions such as the gravity of the offence.

title: Undertrial release — the one-third and half detention rule
text: Section 479 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 requires the court to release an undertrial on bail once they have been in detention for half of the maximum sentence prescribed for the offence (excluding death/life-imprisonment offences); a first-time offender with no prior conviction must be released on bond once they have undergone detention for one-third of that maximum sentence. This is meant to prevent long pre-trial incarceration for those who have not yet been convicted, and applies automatically once the detention threshold is reached, subject to the court's power to hear the prosecution first.

title: How to complain against a police officer's misconduct
text: A complaint against police misconduct — refusal to register an FIR, demanding a bribe, custodial mistreatment, or similar — can be made in writing to the Superintendent of Police (or Commissioner in a city with commissionerate policing), to the District Magistrate, or to the State Human Rights Commission/National Human Rights Commission for serious violations. Most states also run a police-complaints authority at the district and state level for allegations of serious misconduct. Keep a copy of the complaint and any acknowledgment; where the FIR itself was wrongly refused, the Section 173(4)/175(3) remedies described elsewhere in this guidance apply in parallel.

title: Reporting a missing person
text: A missing-person report can be lodged at any police station — it should be registered as a General/Non-Cognizable Diary entry, and if there is any suspicion of foul play, kidnapping or an offence, it must be registered as an FIR; courts have directed that missing-child complaints in particular be treated seriously and registered as FIRs given the possibility of trafficking or a cognizable offence. Give the police a recent photograph, physical description, last-seen location and time, and any devices/accounts (phone number, social media) the person used, since this information supports tracing efforts.

title: Women Helpline 181 and One Stop Centres
text: The Women Helpline (181) is a 24x7 telephonic service under the Ministry of Women and Child Development's Mission Shakti scheme that links women facing violence — in public or private spaces — to the police, hospitals, One Stop Centres and legal aid services. One Stop Centres (OSCs), set up in every district since 2015, provide medical aid, police assistance, legal aid, temporary shelter (women and their children can stay up to five days) and psycho-social counselling under one roof, free of cost, to women affected by violence.

title: Filing a domestic violence complaint — Protection Officer and Magistrate route
text: Under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, an aggrieved woman (or a Protection Officer or any other person on her behalf) can present an application to the Magistrate under Section 12 seeking relief, and the Magistrate considers any domestic incident report from the Protection Officer before passing orders. Section 18 lets the Magistrate pass a protection order barring further violence, entry to the workplace, or contact, while Section 17 guarantees the woman's right to reside in the shared household regardless of ownership. Every district has a Protection Officer who can be approached directly to start this process, along with registered service providers and the 181 helpline.

title: Filing a workplace sexual harassment complaint (POSH)
text: Under Section 9 of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013, an aggrieved woman must ordinarily file a written complaint with the workplace's Internal Committee (or the Local Committee if the employer has not constituted one, such as for very small establishments) within three months of the incident, extendable to six months from the last incident in a series if the Committee is satisfied there was sufficient cause for delay. If she cannot write the complaint herself, any Committee member must render reasonable assistance. Section 11 requires the inquiry to follow the applicable service rules or, absent such rules, a prescribed procedure.

title: Reporting dowry harassment and cruelty
text: Cruelty by a husband or his relatives, including dowry-related harassment, is a cognizable criminal offence and can be reported at any police station as a Zero FIR under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, or you may approach the Women Helpline (181), the local Mahila Thana (women's police station) where one exists, or the National Commission for Women's online complaint system. A woman can simultaneously seek civil remedies (protection/residence/maintenance orders) under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 through the local Protection Officer, alongside the criminal complaint.

title: 112 — India's single emergency number
text: Dialling 112 connects you to the Emergency Response Support System (ERSS), a pan-India single number replacing separate police, fire and ambulance lines; the system uses automatic location identification so you do not need to explain exactly where you are, and dispatches the nearest available police van, ambulance or fire unit. You can also reach ERSS by SMS, the 112 India mobile app's SOS button, or web request; the app additionally has a SHOUT feature that alerts nearby registered volunteers, which can be useful in a women's safety emergency.

title: Free legal aid for women — available regardless of income
text: Under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, women are among the categories entitled to free legal services from the National/State/District Legal Services Authority irrespective of their income — unlike most other applicants, who must meet an income-eligibility ceiling. This covers free representation by a lawyer, help with drafting applications, court-fee exemptions where applicable, and guidance through the process. Approach the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) in your district court complex, or call the NALSA toll-free helpline 15100, or apply online through the National Legal Services Authority's portal.

title: Claiming maintenance for a wife, children or parents
text: Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 lets a Magistrate of the first class order a person with sufficient means, who neglects or refuses to maintain his wife (unable to maintain herself), his minor or dependent children, or his aged/infirm parents, to pay a monthly allowance. An application is filed before the Magistrate in the district where the applicant resides; this criminal-law remedy exists alongside maintenance rights available under personal laws (such as the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955) and can be pursued through a lawyer or with help from the District Legal Services Authority.

title: Maternity leave and workplace rights overview
text: The Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 (as amended in 2017) entitles an eligible woman employee to 26 weeks of paid maternity leave for her first two children (12 weeks for the third child onward), work-from-home options where the nature of work permits after the leave period, and protection from dismissal during pregnancy/maternity leave. Employers with 50 or more employees must also provide crèche facilities. A woman denied these benefits can complain to the labour inspector/Assistant Labour Commissioner in her area, or seek help from the local labour department; this is separate from, and in addition to, POSH protections against workplace harassment.

title: Where to complain — District, State or National Consumer Commission
text: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which forum hears your case depends on the value of the goods or services paid as consideration: the District Commission has jurisdiction up to Rupees one crore (Section 34), the State Commission for claims above one crore up to ten crore (Section 47), and the National Commission for claims above ten crore (Section 58). Complaints against unfair contracts up to ten crore also go to the State Commission, and above that to the National Commission. File in the District Commission within whose limits the opposite party resides or carries on business, or where the cause of action arose.

title: Filing a consumer complaint online through e-Daakhil
text: e-Daakhil (edaakhil.nic.in), run under the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, lets a consumer or their advocate file a case in the District, State or National Consumer Commission without visiting in person. Register on the portal (an OTP is sent to your registered mobile number or an activation link to your email), select the appropriate commission and case type, fill in the complaint details and relief sought, upload supporting documents (bill, correspondence, etc.), pay the prescribed fee online, and submit — the portal lets you track the case status afterwards. It is now operational in every state and union territory.

title: National Consumer Helpline (1915)
text: The National Consumer Helpline, reachable on the toll-free number 1915 (8 AM to 8 PM) or WhatsApp on +91-88000-01915, is run by the Department of Consumer Affairs to help consumers register grievances, get guidance, and track resolution — it also offers a web portal, mobile app and the UMANG app. It is a grievance-redressal and mediation-facilitation channel, not itself a consumer court; complaints unresolved through the helpline can still be escalated to the District, State or National Consumer Commission or filed via e-Daakhil.

title: What you need before filing a consumer complaint
text: Before filing, keep the purchase bill/invoice, warranty card, any written communication with the seller or service provider, and proof that you first tried to resolve the issue with them. Section 69 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 requires a complaint to be filed within two years from the date the cause of action arose; a delay can still be condoned if the Commission is satisfied there was sufficient cause, but this is not guaranteed, so timely filing matters. A demand/legal notice to the opposite party before filing, while not always mandatory, strengthens the complaint and shows the grievance was raised.

title: Escalating an e-commerce complaint — grievance officer first
text: Under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 (made under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019), every e-commerce entity must appoint a grievance officer who must acknowledge a complaint within 48 hours and redress it within one month of receipt. If the grievance officer does not resolve the issue in time, or you are dissatisfied with the response, you can escalate to the National Consumer Helpline (1915), file a complaint on the INGRAM/consumerhelpline.gov.in portal, or approach the appropriate Consumer Commission depending on the value involved.

title: Complaining about a false or misleading advertisement
text: The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) can, on being satisfied that an advertisement is false or misleading and prejudicial to consumer interest, direct the advertiser, manufacturer, endorser or publisher to discontinue or modify it, and can impose penalties (Section 21, Consumer Protection Act, 2019). Section 89 separately makes causing a false or misleading advertisement a punishable offence — up to two years' imprisonment and Rs 10 lakh fine for a first offence, rising for repeat offences. Complaints can be filed with the CCPA, the National Consumer Helpline (1915), or the consumerhelpline.gov.in portal.

title: Product liability — claiming compensation for a defective/harmful product
text: Chapter VI (Sections 82 onward) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 lets a consumer claim compensation for harm caused by a defective product from the manufacturer, the product service provider, or in some cases the seller — for example where the seller exercised substantial control over the product's design, manufacturing or packaging, or gave an independent express warranty that was not honoured (Section 86). Such a claim can be brought before the appropriate Consumer Commission along with, or instead of, a regular deficiency-of-service complaint, depending on the facts of the harm caused.

title: Escalating a wrongly rejected insurance claim
text: If an insurer rejects or delays your claim without adequate reason, first file a written complaint with the insurer's own Grievance Redressal Officer; if unresolved within the insurer's stipulated timeline (commonly 30 days) or the response is unsatisfactory, you can approach the Insurance Ombudsman for claims up to Rs 50 lakh, a forum set up under the Insurance Ombudsman Rules for a free, fast, non-court resolution. You may also complain to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) through its Integrated Grievance Management System, or file a consumer complaint before the appropriate Consumer Commission as a deficiency of service.

title: How to file an RTI request
text: Section 6 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 lets any person request information in writing or by electronic means, in English, Hindi or the area's official language, addressed to the Public Information Officer (PIO) of the concerned public authority, along with the prescribed fee. Under the Central RTI Rules, 2012, the fee for requests to central government authorities is Rs 10, payable in cash, by demand draft/banker's cheque/postal order, or electronically where the authority permits; you do not need to give any reason for wanting the information.

title: RTI reply timelines — 30 days, and 48 hours for life or liberty
text: Section 7(1) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 requires the Public Information Officer to provide the information or reject the request (citing reasons under Sections 8/9) as expeditiously as possible, and in any case within thirty days of receiving it; if the information concerns the life or liberty of a person, it must be provided within forty-eight hours. Failure to decide within the specified period is deemed a refusal under Section 7(2), which lets you file a first appeal even without a formal rejection order.

title: RTI first appeal — within 30 days
text: If you receive no decision within the time specified under Section 7 of the Right to Information Act, 2005, or are dissatisfied with the decision, Section 19(1) lets you file a first appeal within thirty days of the expiry of that period or of receiving the decision, to an officer senior in rank to the Public Information Officer within the same public authority. The appellate officer may admit a late appeal if satisfied there was sufficient cause for the delay. No fee is prescribed under the Act itself for this first appeal.

title: RTI second appeal — to the Information Commission
text: Section 19(3) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 allows a second appeal, within ninety days of the date the first-appeal decision should have or did come, to the Central Information Commission (for central authorities) or the State Information Commission (for state authorities). The Commission can direct the authority to furnish the information, and Section 20 empowers it to impose a penalty of Rs 250 per day of delay (subject to a ceiling of Rs 25,000) on a Public Information Officer who, without reasonable cause, refused or delayed a request or gave incorrect/incomplete/misleading information.

title: RTI fee exemption for applicants below the poverty line
text: Rule 5 of the Central RTI Rules, 2012 provides that no fee under the request or additional-fee provisions can be charged from a person who is below the poverty line (BPL), provided the applicant attaches a copy of the BPL certificate issued by the appropriate government along with the RTI application. Several state RTI Rules carry a similar exemption. This exemption applies to the initial request fee and to any further fee demanded for photocopying or other costs of providing the information, not only to a general filing fee.

title: What information the RTI Act does not require to be disclosed
text: Section 8 of the Right to Information Act, 2005 lists categories exempt from disclosure — information affecting India's sovereignty, security, strategic, scientific or economic interests, or relations with foreign states; information a court has forbidden from being published; information that would breach Parliamentary/legislative privilege; commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property where disclosure would harm a third party's competitive position (unless larger public interest justifies disclosure); and information that would impede an ongoing investigation, among others. Personal information with no public-activity/interest link is also generally exempt.

title: Filing RTI online for central government bodies
text: The RTI Online portal (rtionline.gov.in) lets citizens file an RTI request electronically with most central government ministries, departments and public authorities, pay the fee online, and track the status and any first appeal against the same request on the portal itself. It works only for central public authorities registered on the portal — for state government departments, you generally need to use the concerned state's own RTI portal (where available) or file physically/by post to that authority's PIO.

title: Cheque bounce — demand notice and complaint timeline
text: When a cheque is returned unpaid, the payee must send a written demand notice to the drawer within 30 days of receiving the bank's return memo. The drawer then has 15 days from receipt of the notice to pay. If payment is not made, a complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 must be filed within one month after that 15-day period ends, before the Magistrate where the payee's bank branch is located. Courts may order interim compensation up to 20 percent of the cheque amount under Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

title: Where to file a cheque-bounce complaint
text: A complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is filed as a criminal complaint before the Court of a Magistrate of the First Class (or higher) exercising jurisdiction over the area where the payee's bank branch — the branch in which the cheque was presented for collection — is situated; this is a special jurisdiction rule that lets the payee sue near their own bank rather than travel to the drawer's location. The complaint must be accompanied by the dishonoured cheque, the bank's return memo, the demand notice, and proof of its service on the drawer.
tags: cheque bounce case where to file

title: Interim compensation in a cheque-bounce case
text: Section 143A of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 lets the trial court order the drawer to pay the complainant interim compensation — up to 20 percent of the cheque amount — either when the accused pleads not guilty in a summary trial/summons case, or upon framing of charge in other cases. This amount must ordinarily be paid within sixty days of the order (extendable by a further thirty days for sufficient cause), and is meant to give the complainant some relief while the case is still being tried, without waiting for final conviction and sentencing.

title: Appeal deposit in a cheque-bounce conviction
text: Section 148 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 requires a drawer appealing against a Section 138 conviction to deposit a minimum of 20 percent of the fine or compensation amount awarded by the trial court, in addition to any interim compensation already paid under Section 143A, ordinarily within sixty days of the appellate court's order (extendable by a further thirty days for sufficient cause). This deposit requirement was added to discourage delay tactics by convicted drawers and to ensure the complainant has some recourse to funds while the appeal is pending.

title: Sending a legal notice — the basics
text: A legal notice is a formal written communication (typically drafted by an advocate) informing the recipient of a grievance and the sender's intended legal action if it is not resolved; for a cheque-bounce case, sending this notice within 30 days of the return memo is a mandatory precondition under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, and it is common practice in many other civil disputes even where not legally mandatory, since it puts the claim on record and can prompt an out-of-court settlement. Send it by a mode that gives proof of delivery (registered post/speed post/courier with tracking, or email with read receipt where accepted), and keep a copy along with the delivery proof.

title: Recovering money owed to you — the small-cause/civil suit route
text: A simple money-recovery claim (an unpaid loan, unreturned deposit, or similar debt not tied to a cheque) is ordinarily pursued as a civil suit for recovery of money in the court having pecuniary and territorial jurisdiction, or, for smaller claims in cities where such courts exist, before the Court of Small Causes, which follows a simpler and faster procedure than a regular civil suit. Before suing, send a legal notice demanding payment; if there is a signed acknowledgment of debt or a cheque/promissory note involved, mention it, as documentary proof of the debt substantially speeds up recovery.

title: After a road accident — FIR and the Detailed Accident Report
text: Report a road accident involving injury, death or significant damage to the nearest police station so an FIR can be registered (a Zero FIR can be filed at any station under Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 if the accident occurred elsewhere). The investigating officer is required to prepare a Detailed Accident Report (DAR) — including details of the vehicles, parties, and injuries — within a set period, and forward it to the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, which can treat it as an application for compensation even before the victim/family files one separately.

title: Filing a compensation claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal
text: Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 lets a person injured in an accident, the owner of damaged property, or (where death resulted) the legal representatives of the deceased, apply for compensation before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) of the area where the accident occurred, or where the claimant resides/carries on business, or where the defendant resides. No court fee is charged on such an application, and the claim can be filed even without engaging a lawyer, though legal help is recommended for computing compensation correctly and dealing with the insurer.

title: Compensation for hit-and-run accidents
text: Section 161 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 requires the Central Government to pay compensation, under a scheme it notifies, for death or grievous hurt caused by a hit-and-run motor accident — that is, where the identity of the offending vehicle cannot be established. This is a fixed-sum compensation scheme distinct from a regular MACT claim against an identified vehicle/insurer, since there is no traceable driver or insurer to claim against; applications are made to the district authorities/claims tribunal designated for the scheme, generally supported by the police FIR/report on the hit-and-run incident.

title: Good Samaritan protection for helping accident victims
text: Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 protects a Good Samaritan — a person who, in good faith and without expectation of reward, renders emergency medical or non-medical assistance to an accident victim — from civil or criminal liability for any injury or death that results from their negligence while giving that assistance. This means a bystander who takes an accident victim to hospital or gives first aid cannot be forced to become a witness or be harassed by police/hospital staff merely for helping; the Central Government has also issued rules on how such a person may be questioned, if at all.

title: Third-party motor insurance is legally compulsory
text: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 makes it mandatory for every vehicle used in a public place to be covered by at least a third-party liability insurance policy, which compensates injury/death/property damage caused to others by that vehicle, regardless of whether the vehicle owner also has comprehensive (own-damage) cover. Driving without valid third-party insurance is itself a punishable offence, separate from any compensation liability, and victims of an accident caused by an uninsured or untraced vehicle can still claim through the hit-and-run compensation scheme or the Motor Vehicle Accident Fund route for identified but uninsured vehicles.

title: Checking and contesting an e-challan
text: Traffic e-challans issued under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 can be checked and paid online at echallan.parivahan.gov.in (or the relevant state traffic police portal/app) using the challan number or vehicle registration number. If you believe a challan was wrongly issued — wrong vehicle, expired offence, or a technical error — most portals let you submit a grievance/dispute online, or you may need to appear before the concerned virtual/traffic court on the notice date to contest it; ignoring an unpaid challan can lead to it being escalated to a court notice for adjudication.

title: Driving licence and RC on DigiLocker/mParivahan are legally valid
text: The Ministry of Road Transport & Highways has directed all enforcement authorities to accept a Driving Licence, Registration Certificate or other transport document presented in electronic form through DigiLocker or the mParivahan app as valid — such electronic records are treated as legally equivalent to the original physical document under the Information Technology Act, 2000, provided they are shown from the DigiLocker or mParivahan platform itself (a photo or PDF saved elsewhere on the phone does not carry the same legal status). Real-time RC/DL/fitness/insurance/permit validity can also be checked on the mParivahan app by entering the vehicle or licence number.

title: Penalties for drunk or drugged driving
text: Section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 punishes driving or attempting to drive with more than 30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood (as detected by a breathalyser or other test), or while under the influence of a drug to an extent that impairs proper control of the vehicle. A first offence attracts imprisonment up to six months and/or a fine (Rs 10,000 under the current fine schedule); a second or subsequent offence within three years attracts enhanced imprisonment and fine. This is independent of any separate liability for an accident caused while driving in this state.

title: Who is eligible for free legal aid under NALSA
text: Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 entitles specific categories to free legal services regardless of income — including women and children, members of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, victims of trafficking or begar, persons with disabilities, victims of mass disaster/violence/flood/drought/earthquake, industrial workmen, persons in custody, and persons in receivership. Anyone else is eligible if their annual income is below the limit prescribed by their State Legal Services Authority. Free legal aid covers a lawyer's fees, cost of drafting and filing documents, and process/incidental costs, applied for through the District Legal Services Authority (DLSA).

title: Lok Adalat — quick, free, no-appeal dispute settlement
text: A Lok Adalat, organised under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, is a forum for amicable settlement of disputes — both pending court cases (referred with the parties' consent) and disputes at the pre-litigation stage — through conciliation rather than adversarial adjudication. There is no court fee for a Lok Adalat, and any court fee already paid on a case referred there is refunded if it settles; an award passed has the force of a civil court decree and is final, with no appeal against it. National Lok Adalats are held periodically across all district courts on notified dates.

title: Plea bargaining — how it works
text: Chapter XXIII of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (Section 289 onward) lets an accused apply for plea bargaining in cases where the police report or the Magistrate's cognizance does not involve an offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding seven years, and the offence does not affect the socio-economic condition of the country or was not committed against a woman or a child below 14. The accused files an application voluntarily, disclosing the facts, and the court works out a mutually satisfactory disposition (often a reduced sentence) with the prosecution and victim; this is different from an acquittal and results in a conviction on a lesser sentence.

title: Engaging an advocate, and complaining about one
text: Any person may engage a practising advocate enrolled with a State Bar Council to represent them in court; fees are generally negotiated directly with the advocate (subject to Bar Council of India rules), and a written engagement letter/vakalatnama is signed for court representation. If an advocate is guilty of professional misconduct — such as not appearing despite being paid, or ethical violations — a complaint (a petition, with the prescribed fee) can be filed with the State Bar Council, which registers it and may refer it to a Disciplinary Committee; the Committee, after hearing both sides, can reprimand, suspend, or remove the advocate from the roll.

title: Checking your court case status online (eCourts)
text: The eCourts Services portal (services.ecourts.gov.in), run by the e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India through the National Informatics Centre, lets you check case status, cause lists, and daily orders for district and taluka courts across India, using the case's CNR (Case Number Record) — a unique 16-character code assigned to every case — or by searching with the case registration number, party name, or advocate name. The same services are available through the eCourts Services mobile app on Android and iOS, without needing to visit the court in person just to know the next hearing date.

title: Limitation periods — why filing on time matters
text: The Limitation Act, 1963 fixes time limits within which a civil suit, appeal or application must be filed — for example, three years for most contract/money-recovery suits from when the right to sue accrues; specific statutes carry their own limitation rules for other proceedings, such as two years for a consumer complaint (Section 69, Consumer Protection Act, 2019) or thirty days for an RTI first appeal (Section 19, RTI Act, 2005). Filing after the limitation period generally bars the claim outright, though courts can condone delay in many civil matters if satisfied there was sufficient cause — so acting quickly once a cause of action arises is important.

title: Anticipatory bail — protection before arrest
text: Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 lets a person who has reason to believe they may be arrested for a non-bailable offence apply to the Court of Session or the High Court for a direction that, if arrested, they be released on bail. The court can attach conditions — such as making oneself available for police interrogation, not tampering with evidence or influencing witnesses, and not leaving the country without permission — and can grant this protection even before any FIR is registered, based on a genuine apprehension of arrest.

title: Mediation for family and matrimonial disputes
text: Family courts and district courts across India commonly refer matrimonial and family disputes — including divorce, custody, and maintenance disagreements — to court-annexed mediation centres before or during litigation, aiming for a mutually agreed settlement rather than a contested judgment; several High Courts and the Supreme Court's Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee have set up such centres, and the Legal Services Authorities also facilitate mediation and Lok Adalats for family matters. Mediation is voluntary, confidential, and — if successful — the settlement can be recorded by the court, giving it legal effect, without either party having to "win" an adversarial case.

title: Maintenance Tribunal for senior citizens and parents
text: Under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, a senior citizen or parent unable to maintain themselves from their own income or property can apply for maintenance from their children or relatives before a Maintenance Tribunal (usually headed by the Sub-Divisional Magistrate) in their district; the application can also be filed by another person or a registered organisation on their behalf if they are unable to do so themselves. Filing is free of cost, and the Tribunal is required to dispose of the application within ninety days of notice being served on the respondent, extendable by a further thirty days for recorded reasons.
